title: jstrain drill bank: JS and Node fluency under time
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 bank-jstrain row). Scope = jstrain modules 01-29 and the quiz modules (the ts-* modules belong to the TypeScript practice, not this list). Sources and siblings are live jstrain drills of the modules that teach the idea. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Under time pressure, answer two questions first: which variable does this closure hold, and what is this at the call site? Most trick snippets turn on one of them.
ideas.why: Timed exercises and interview snippets are built around stale closures and lost this; guessing costs more time than tracing those two facts.
ideas.prompt: In a timed round you see a factory that returns three validator functions built in a loop, and a method passed to setTimeout. Both misbehave. What do you trace in each, in what order?
ideas.answer: For the validators, find which binding each function closes over: one shared var means they all see its final value; a fresh binding per iteration fixes it. For the timer, ask who calls the method: setTimeout calls a bare function, so this is lost unless it was bound or wrapped in an arrow.

ideas.idea: Three async tools come up again and again: a pool that caps concurrency, a retry with growing jittered backoff, and a timeout that aborts the work through an AbortSignal.
ideas.why: Unbounded Promise.all overloads a partner API, retries without backoff become a storm, and a timeout that only stops waiting leaves the request running.
ideas.prompt: You must call a flaky partner API for 5,000 ids. It allows 10 concurrent requests, fails about 2% of calls transiently, and a call that takes over 3 seconds is useless. Describe the code you would write.
ideas.answer: Run the ids through a pool of 10 workers, so at most 10 calls are in flight. Wrap each call in a retry whose waits grow exponentially, capped and randomised, retrying only transient failures a few times. Give each attempt an AbortSignal with a 3-second timeout, so a slow call is cancelled, not just abandoned.

ideas.idea: Before changing buggy code, write down the input that breaks it and get a test to fail on it; fix only when you can watch that test turn green.
ideas.why: A fix without a reproduction is a guess: it may cure a different case, and nothing stops the bug from coming back.
ideas.prompt: A bug report says 'the leaderboard order is sometimes wrong'. You see a suspicious sort comparator. Why not just rewrite the comparator, and what do you do first?
ideas.answer: Find the input that breaks it first, for example equal scores or scores above 9 sorting as text, and write a failing test with exactly that data. Then change the comparator and watch the test pass. The test proves the cause was found and keeps it from returning.

ideas.idea: A good test fails when the code is subtly wrong: aim tests at boundaries, empty inputs, later elements and error paths, where small mistakes hide.
ideas.why: Tests that only check the happy middle pass against code with an off-by-one or a missing branch, so they give confidence they have not earned.
ideas.prompt: `inRange(x, lo, hi)` has three tests, all with x in the middle of the range. Someone changes <= to < and every test still passes. Which tests should have existed?
ideas.answer: Tests at the edges: x equal to lo, x equal to hi, and one just outside each end. A strict-less-than mutant fails the hi test at once. The same habit applies elsewhere: the empty list, duplicates that are not adjacent, and the second word of a title.

ideas.idea: Hunt for the classic holes where input meets power: SQL built from strings, file paths built from user input, object merges that accept special keys.
ideas.why: These bugs look like ordinary code and pass every functional test, yet each one hands an attacker data or control.
ideas.prompt: A file-download handler joins a base folder with `req.query.name`, and a search builds `WHERE name LIKE '%${q}%'`. Name the attack on each and the fix.
ideas.answer: The download is path traversal: a name with '../' segments escapes the folder; resolve the full path and refuse anything outside the base directory. The search is SQL injection: a quote in q rewrites the query; pass q as a bound parameter. The same review catches merges that copy '__proto__' into objects.

ideas.idea: Write files atomically (write a temporary file, then rename over the old one) and pass values to SQL as parameters inside a transaction.
ideas.why: A crash during a plain overwrite leaves a half-written file, and string-built SQL is both an injection hole and a source of quoting bugs.
ideas.prompt: A CLI keeps its data in data.json, overwriting it with writeFileSync on every change. After a power cut the file is empty and the app refuses to start. How do you make saving safe?
ideas.answer: Write the new contents to a temporary file in the same directory, flush it, then rename it over data.json: the rename replaces the file in one step, so readers see the old version or the new one, never half of each. If the data moves to SQLite, use bound parameters and wrap related writes in a transaction.

ideas.idea: Choose the data structure from the operation mix: a map for lookups, a heap for repeated minimum or maximum, a real queue instead of shift(), an LRU for bounded caches.
ideas.why: The wrong structure turns a fast operation into a scan, so code that passes small tests times out on real input.
ideas.prompt: A job scheduler keeps tasks in an array, sorts it after each insert, and takes the first element with shift(). With 100,000 tasks it crawls. What structure fits, and why?
ideas.answer: The operations are 'insert' and 'take the earliest', which is a priority queue: a binary min-heap does both in logarithmic time instead of a sort per insert. shift() also re-indexes the whole array each time. If tasks are looked up by id as well, keep a map from id to task beside the heap.
